papers.title: What Kind of Suffering Does Meditation Reduce?
papers.abstract: Meditation has been shown to reduce various forms of suffering and increase well-being. However, its broad effectiveness raises the question: In what way does meditation reduce suffering? We explore this question systematically, proposing that meditation’s effectiveness stems not from addressing specific types of suffering but from dismantling underlying mechanisms that create the conditions for suffering. First, we examine suffering from three frameworks: well-being (hedonia/eudaimonia), contemporary mindfulness (non-reactivity), and traditional Buddhist practice (ignorance). While these approaches may correspond to phenomenologically similar states with less suffering, they reinforce different underlying habits, thereby affecting the likelihood of future suffering. Second, we clarify this distinction by drawing on the action–perception cycle from a computational phenomenology perspective. Particularly, we cast suffering as self-reinforcing action–perception cycles, and unreliable/reliable reduction of suffering as unstable/stable equilibrium in action–perception cycles. Third, we propose four stages through which meditation facilitates a reliable reduction by progressively revealing that suffering, typically perceived as a passive experience, is in fact a specific pattern of action we are engaged in (i.e. meditation provides a reliable way to reduce enacted suffering). Our framework provides a conceptual foundation for mathematically formalizing and computationally modelling non-reactivity, ignorance (in the Buddhist sense), and suffering, and has implications for the larger goal of understanding perception, action, and conscious experience.

papers.title: School Nurse-Led Mindfulness Activities for Third-Grade Children.
papers.abstract: School nurses are uniquely positioned to support students' social and emotional well-being through school-based interventions. A school nurse-led quality improvement initiative introduced mindfulness interventions for third-grade students to support self-awareness and self-regulation in alignment with the Illinois State Board of Education Social and Emotional Learning Standards. The intervention included 15 video mindfulness lessons delivered to third-grade teachers for classroom use over 4 weeks. Students learned to develop self-awareness and self-regulation skills using tools such as breathing boards, relaxation, and the five senses. Sixty-five students completed pre- and post-social, academic, and emotional assessments; their social risk scores improved, indicating a reduction in perceived social risk. Teachers and students provided positive feedback on the activities and how they benefited from the lessons. Our results indicate that school nurse-led mindfulness interventions are a feasible strategy that may improve students' social well-being and self-regulation skills.

papers.title: Brain Reorganization Following Psychological Interventions for Chronic Pain: A Systematic Review of Neuroimaging Evidence.
papers.abstract: Psychological interventions are effective for chronic pain, but their neural mechanisms remain unclear. This review synthesized functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography evidence on treatment-related brain changes following psychological interventions in adults with chronic non-cancer pain. Seven databases were searched. Eligible studies included adults aged 18-64 receiving a psychological intervention with both neuroimaging and clinical outcomes. Study quality was assessed with the Effective Public Health Practice Project tool. Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis, findings were synthesized narratively. Nineteen studies (n = 843) were included: 15 randomized controlled trials, 3 within-subject designs, and 1 pilot non-randomized trial. Interventions were mindfulness-based interventions (n = 6), cognitive behavioral therapy (n = 5), hypnosis (n = 3), neurofeedback (n = 3), and other approaches (n = 2). The anterior insula, anterior cingulate and midcingulate cortex, prefrontal cortex, and primary somatosensory cortex were most consistently implicated. Cognitive behavioral therapy reduced somatosensory-limbic coupling and enhanced prefrontal engagement. Mindfulness showed convergent insular and cingulate involvement. Pain reprocessing therapy showed close alignment between observed neural changes and its proposed mechanism, with reduced affective-evaluative pain activation and increased prefrontal-somatosensory connectivity. Hypnosis dissociated somatosensory from affective pain processing. Brain-behavior correlations linked predominantly to cognitive-affective outcomes, including catastrophizing, self-efficacy, and anxiety rather than pain intensity. Across interventions, convergent findings implicated increased prefrontal engagement and reduced affective-evaluative pain processing, broadly consistent with cognitive-affective modulation of pain. These findings offer neurobiological plausibility for clinical approaches targeting catastrophizing and fear-avoidance, though guiding patient selection would require research linking neural change directly to clinical outcome. PERSPECTIVE: This review identified shared neuroanatomical hubs, including increased prefrontal regulation and reduced affective-evaluative pain processing across cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness, hypnosis, and pain reprocessing therapy. These findings provide neurobiological support for established clinical approaches targeting cognitive-affective responses to pain, but do not establish shared causal mechanisms or support patient stratification. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This systematic review was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (registration number: CRD42024623019).
